svg.aria-label: The accuracy splicing demands and how it is achieved: the frameshift and premature stop codon that follow if an exon boundary slips by one base, the scale problem of finding two points among tens of thousands of bases, and the use of several weak signals in combination rather than one strong sequence, which leaves room for regulation.
svg.text: A One base off, and everything after it changes
correct join
...A U G G C A U U C A A G C C U...
Met - Ala - Phe - Lys - Pro
joined one base late
...A U G G C A U U C C A A G C C U...
Met - Ala - Phe - Gln - Ala - ... every codon after the join differs
a stop codon soon appears
result: a short useless protein, or the transcript is cleared by nonsense-mediated decay
B The scale of the search
About 8 introns per human gene, and most of the length is intron.
Two exact points must be found among tens of thousands of bases,
with no margin of even one base.
C How, and what it leaves open
Not one long specific sequence, but several SHORT weak
signals plus the RNA and protein interactions that read them.
combined, they locate the site
A weak signal is not a flaw — it is the room for control.
If the signal were absolute, the cut would always be the same.
Because it is weak, regulators can change the choice: alternative splicing.
